connection_type: I have direct personal experience (as an immigrant, refugee, religious minority, or member of a marginalised group)
disclosure_text: I grew up in Lagos, Nigeria and only moved to Canada when I was 17. I am 31 now and i had to go through the process of being on a study visa/permit, to a post graduate work permit, to a permanent resident and finally to a canadian citizen.
micronarrative:
There was a time at my workplace where I was told as an international student, I was only allowed to work 20 hours per week. This was odd because as an international student, we needed the money the most to pay our fees. It made me feel helpless and distraught. I had to fight for the 20 hours to make sure I made as much money as possible.

I had a conversation with my manager where I expressed my displeasure to him. He made me understand that there was nothing he could do and that the decision had come from above him from Immigration Canada. I didn't feel great at all. I took it in good faith because, in all honesty, I saw it coming. I tried to corner him, but he wouldn't budge. The tension was palpable, and it felt like the discrimination against international students was being ignored, even in my own workplace.

annotations.rationale: The phrase “oppression with extra steps” is rhetorical shorthand. It suggests that instead of reducing social divisions, intersectional thinking may multiply them by continually subdividing people into categories. Whether someone sees the framework as clarifying or fragmenting often depends on: how it is applied institutionally, whether it leaves room for shared identity and common ground, and whether it’s used analytically versus morally.
